html:
SMTO-DB-0003 — SMTO's database tool only works with PostgreSQL databases

GUID: 9443c00f-9abf-4962-b2b9-9c69940f6508
Slug: database-backend-unsupported
Domain: DB · Subsystem: db

What happened

  • The database SMTO was asked to use looks like a kind other than PostgreSQL, and SMTO's built-in database tool can only talk to PostgreSQL. No query was run.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. Find out what kind of database it is. If it's not PostgreSQL (for example MySQL, SQLite or Oracle), ask the person who manages SMTO whether another Skill is set up for it. This tool cannot read other kinds of databases, so changing the request won't help.
  2. If it is PostgreSQL, open Parameter Store, select the entry, and remove any other database name, such as "mysql", from its description, tags and aliases. Select Save. SMTO guesses the kind of database from these words, so a stray name makes it think it's a different kind.
  3. On the entry's Value tab, select Reveal & edit value and remove any file path field, or set an engine field to postgresql, then select Save. A file path makes SMTO treat the entry as a SQLite file instead of a PostgreSQL server.
  4. In the conversation, type @, pick the corrected entry, and ask your question again. SMTO then reads the entry's corrected details instead of the old ones.

What success looks like

  • SMTO connects to the database and answers your question instead of showing this error.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO, saying what kind of database you are using. Don't label a non-PostgreSQL database as PostgreSQL to get past this; SMTO would then send it commands it can't understand.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The native database path resolved an engine other than PostgreSQL (from the profile's engine/db_type/driver field, tags, aliases, description or a SQLite path field), or the discovery request or saved database context named a missing or non-PostgreSQL engine.

What this means

  • The database path normalizes its engine and rejects anything other than PostgreSQL; missing engine also blocks discovery admission. Input rejection is pre-dispatch only where the producer says so. Discovery and psql failures require their original execution evidence; diagnostics do not run SQL or prove that a mutation rolled back.

Why this can happen

  • The database path normalizes its engine and rejects anything other than PostgreSQL; missing engine also blocks discovery admission.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect the saved profile engine and normalized discovery engine independently of credentials.

How to fix it

  • Check how parameter_database_profile() classified the Parameter Store entry: an engine/db_type/driver field, or an engine word in tags, aliases or description (for example mysql), overrides the PostgreSQL default, and a database_path/db_path/file field makes it SQLite. Correct those fields if the server really is PostgreSQL; discovery requests must send engine=postgres. Other engines need a separately supported Skill; do not bypass the engine check.
  • Select a PostgreSQL profile or a separately supported capability for the intended backend.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • The chosen operation resolves an explicitly supported PostgreSQL profile.

What not to do

  • Do not bypass the unsupported-feature check or reinterpret an unsupported response as success.

Technical notes

  • Input rejection is pre-dispatch only where the producer says so. Discovery and psql failures require their original execution evidence; diagnostics do not run SQL or prove that a mutation rolled back.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
